en.title: University of Sydney Quadrangle
en.summary: Take a stroll past the sandstone arcades, the clock tower, and the lawn to examine the architectural details of this Gothic Revival-style campus.
en.guide:
## Introduction
The University of Sydney Quadrangle was not built all at once; it evolved through several phases of expansion, beginning in the mid-19th century, to eventually form the enclosed space we see today. Edmund Blacket contributed to the design of the early main building and the Great Hall, while other architects joined the project later—with additions continuing well into the 20th century. With their golden Sydney sandstone, pointed arches, towers, and rows of windows, these structures draw inspiration from the collegiate architecture of British universities—translating the young colonial institution’s aspirations toward academic tradition into a tangible, traversable space. Rather than relying on a single photograph of a façade, one can discover the subtle variations in stone hue, bay rhythm, and architectural detail—each reflecting a different era—by strolling slowly along the arcades.

The central lawn provides a vantage point from which to view the surrounding buildings, while the arcades break down the expansive façades into smaller, intimate segments, inviting the observer to pause and examine individual elements: column capitals, stone carvings, grotesque waterspouts, and arched doorways. The jacaranda trees also serve as a poignant seasonal landmark; after the original, venerable tree fell in 2016, a clone—along with a native Illawarra flame tree—was planted in 2017, joining other jacarandas scattered across the campus. While the blooms arrive and depart with the seasons, the architecture itself offers a rich, enduring visual experience year-round. As a functioning campus dedicated to study, administration, and events, the space remains accessible for casual walks—primarily through the open courtyards and external arcades—where one can respect the rhythms of academic life and ceremonies, all while sensing that this is a historic site deeply embedded in the present-day life of the university.
## How to explore
1. Approach the main building from the direction of University Place. Take in the clock tower, the entrance, and the long façade before entering the courtyard through an open passageway. Spend 10–15 minutes observing how the surrounding buildings relate to the central lawn—and please, avoid stopping in the middle of the passageway for large group photos.
2. Walk halfway around the open cloister, taking time to compare various archways, stone carvings, and windows; notice the overall repetition, then look for the unique details. Enter the Great Hall or the teaching and office spaces only when they are explicitly open to the public; otherwise, the building’s silhouette can be fully appreciated from the outside.
3. Move to the other side of the courtyard to observe the interplay between the vegetation, the light, and the architecture. Find a public seat to rest before heading back the way you came. If there is an event taking place on the lawn or within a section of the cloister, please follow the posted signage to take a detour. If you wish to visit the museum, consider that as a separate, dedicated excursion.
## Timing
Allow 45 minutes to explore the main building’s façade and the cloister; 75–90 minutes will provide enough time for closer inspection of architectural details and a short stroll around the campus. Morning or afternoon sunlight, hitting the structures at an angle, best highlights the texture of the sandstone. If you are visiting during the flowering season, remember to factor in potential wait times for photo opportunities—though the flowers should not be considered the primary focus of your visit.
## Getting there and costs
Take a bus to the vicinity of Parramatta Road or City Road (University of Sydney), then walk to The Quadrangle. Alternatively, you can reach the campus on foot from Redfern Station. Access to general public spaces is free of charge; however, dining, parking, and special events may incur additional costs. When using navigation apps, set your destination to "The Quadrangle" rather than the museum entrance.
## Nearby food
Campus cafés are great for a quick break on weekdays—take a look at the kitchen setup and seating arrangements before placing your order. If options are limited on the weekend, head toward the commercial districts along Broadway or Newtown for a meal. Please consume food only in designated areas; do not use the academic corridors as dining spaces.
en.tips: During graduation ceremonies, examinations, or periods when lawns are cordoned off, please follow the posted detour signs. Do not climb on stone sculptures or place items against the walls of historic buildings. When taking photographs, be mindful to avoid capturing classroom windows or staff at work. Exercise caution on stone steps, as they may be slippery after rain.

items.guide:
## 简介
这里指Sydney Olympic Park内的Bicentennial Park，而非Glebe等地的同名绿地。湖畔草地、湿地、红树林与公共艺术连在一起，让它既适合普通散步，也适合观察城市边缘仍保留和修复的生态环境；从开阔湖面进入木栈道，空间与光线会有明显变化。

Lake Belvedere、Badu Mangroves、鸟类观察点以及Treillage Tower等地标提供不同观看方式。水面可看倒影和鸟类，红树林适合观察根系与潮汐环境，较高位置则帮助理解园区和周围城市的关系。面积较大，选择一条可折返的主题路线，比把每个地标都串成任务更适合轻松到访。
## 这样逛
1. 先确认目的地是Sydney Olympic Park的Bicentennial Park，在现场导览图选Lake Belvedere附近作为起点；不是Glebe湾岸的同名公园。先沿湖边开放路径适应距离和日照。
2. 按指示选择Badu Mangroves的开放木栈道，观察红树林根系与潮汐环境；再选鸟类观察点远看水鸟，不离开步道、不靠近鸟巢。
3. 体力与开放情况允许时，再去Treillage Tower或Peace Monument、Sundial一带看景观和公共艺术。爬塔不是必选，遇维护或身体不适可留在地面；最后回到湖边休息并沿已走过的路线返回。
## 时间怎么用
90分钟湖边加一段红树林步道；180分钟可加观鸟、公共艺术与休息。每天日出至日落开放，园区较大，选择短路线并留足返回交通的时间。
## 怎么去与花费
地址Australia Avenue, Sydney Olympic Park；可按地图比较Concord West或Olympic Park方向的步行/公交接驳。公园普通到访免费；停车需登记车牌且有时限，不能默认全天免费。
## 附近餐饮
园区咖啡与餐饮可按当天开放选择，Olympic Park核心区也有更多用餐选项。带水、防晒和适量点心较实用；若准备野餐，使用允许区域并遵守湿地保护与垃圾处理要求。
items.tips: 狗应牵绳，Badu Mangroves等保护范围禁狗；公园水体禁钓鱼，不喂野生动物。带水、防晒和防蚊用品，红树林栈道湿滑时放慢；烧烤、防火与临时关闭遵守现场指示。

en.title: Bicentennial Park
en.summary: Enjoy a leisurely stroll along the park’s walking trails and around the wetlands, while observing all on-site restrictions for the protected area.
en.guide:
## Introduction
This entry refers to Bicentennial Park within Sydney Olympic Park—not to be confused with other parks of the same name, such as the one in Glebe. Featuring a blend of lakeside lawns, wetlands, mangroves, and public art, the park is ideal for a casual stroll or for observing an ecological environment that has been preserved and restored on the urban fringe. As you transition from the open lakefront onto the wooden boardwalks, you will notice a distinct shift in both space and light.

Landmarks such as Lake Belvedere, the Badu Mangroves, bird-watching spots, and the Treillage Tower offer diverse perspectives. The water’s surface reflects the surroundings and attracts various birds; the mangroves provide a unique look at root systems and tidal dynamics; and higher vantage points help reveal the relationship between the park and the surrounding urban landscape. Given the park’s expansive size, a relaxed visit is best achieved by choosing a thematic, out-and-back route rather than attempting to tick off every landmark as if completing a checklist.
## How to explore
1. First, confirm that your destination is Bicentennial Park in Sydney Olympic Park (not the park of the same name in Glebe). Use the on-site map to select an area near Lake Belvedere as your starting point. Begin by following the open paths along the lake to get a feel for the distances and sunlight exposure.
2. Follow the signs to the wooden boardwalks in the Badu Mangroves to observe the mangrove root systems and the tidal environment. Continue to the bird-watching spots to view waterbirds from a distance—please remain on the designated paths and do not approach any nests.
3. If time, energy, and site accessibility permit, visit the Treillage Tower, the Peace Monument, or the Sundial to take in the scenery and public art. Climbing the tower is optional; if it is closed for maintenance or if you are not feeling up to it, you can simply enjoy the view from the ground. Finally, return to the lakeside to rest before heading back along the path you arrived on.
## Timing
Allow 90 minutes for a walk along the lake and through the mangrove boardwalk; allow 180 minutes if you wish to include bird-watching, viewing public art, and taking breaks. Open daily from sunrise to sunset. The park is quite large, so choose a shorter route and allow sufficient time for your return journey.
## Getting there and costs
Address: Australia Avenue, Sydney Olympic Park. Consult a map to compare walking or public transport options via Concord West or Olympic Park stations. General entry to the park is free; however, parking requires vehicle registration and is subject to time limits—do not assume it is free for the entire day.
## Nearby food
Check which cafés and eateries are open on the day of your visit; additional dining options are available in the core Olympic Park precinct. It is advisable to bring water, sun protection, and some snacks. If you plan to have a picnic, please use designated areas and adhere to guidelines regarding wetland conservation and waste disposal.
en.tips: Dogs must be kept on a leash; they are prohibited in protected zones such as the Badu Mangroves. Fishing is not permitted in the park’s waterways, and please do not feed the wildlife. Bring water, sun protection, and insect repellent. Take extra care on the mangrove boardwalks, as they may become slippery. Follow all on-site instructions regarding barbecues, fire safety, and any temporary closures.
